question: The Italian Parliament's inspections of the country's pre-removal centre (CPR) in Gjadër (Albania) have revealed that a number of people had been transferred there even though it was obvious that they had psychiatric issues.

There are reports of similar incidents in CPRs in Italy, the latest of which concerns a citizen who was detained for seven months in Milan before being deported to Albania1, a move which further curtails his right to access healthcare. Data from the Italian Government2 show that, between May and October, more than 13 % of CPR detainees were released on health grounds, in many cases only a few days after arrival.
These transfers raise major concerns about whether the the principle of equal treatment and the detainees’ fundamental rights are being upheld. In the light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of the transfer of people with psychiatric issues to Albania and the criteria on which these decisions are based?

Does it consider that transferring people with mental health problems to Albania and detaining them in CPRs there is a course of action which complies with the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union and EU law?

What measures will the Commission take to make sure that vulnerable people are neither detained in conditions that are likely to aggravate their mental health problems nor transferred to facilities outside the European Union?
Supporter3
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.4.2026) The Commission is aware that, under the Italy-Albania Protocol, Italian authorities are transferring third-country nationals subject to a return decision to the centre in Gjadër for the purpose detention pending removal.

Concerning the EU legal framework relevant to the protocol, the replies provided to previous parliamentary questions already contained relevant elements1. The detention of illegally staying third-country nationals is regulated at EU level by Directive 2008/115/EC (the ‘Return Directive’2).

Articles 1 and 5 of that Directive state that Member States shall take due account of the state of health of the third-country national concerned and ensure that the procedures applied for returning illegally staying third-country nationals are in accordance with fundamental rights.

In relation to detention, the Return Directive3 provides that particular attention shall be paid to the situation of vulnerable persons and that emergency health care and essential treatment of illness shall be provided. Member States are primarily responsible for the implementation of national law implementing the EU legal framework.

The Commission is in contact with the Italian authorities on migration management, including on the implementation of the Italy-Albania protocol dialogue. Member States are responsible for the organisation and delivery of health services and medical care, in accordance with Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union4.
The EU's role in those fields is to complement national policies and encourage knowledge sharing and coordination between Member States.

1 P-002206/2024, E-001425/2025 and E-001648/2025. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=celex:32008L0115. 3 Article 16(3) of the Return Directive. 4 http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:12012E/TXT&from=EN.
